setup: Most history sets the scene and gets going. This story has to start with a fight about itself. Al-Andalus is the Arabic name for whatever part of Spain and Portugal was under Muslim rule between 711 and 1492, and it is the one civilization the modern world genuinely cannot stop arguing about — because too many people need it to have been something. Arab and Muslim writers need it to have been a lost golden age. Jewish historians need it to have been the high-water mark of the diaspora. Liberal multiculturalists need it to have been proof that three faiths can build something glorious together. And a loud counter-camp needs it to have been a colonial occupation dressed up as tolerance. The polite name for the quarrel is the convivencia debate — did Muslims, Christians, and Jews actually live together? — and almost nobody is neutral. This chapter sets the ground: the geography (a strait only eight miles wide, the one crossable land border between Islam and Latin Christendom for eight centuries), the shaky sources, and the shattered Mediterranean of the year 700, ruled at its far western edge by an eighty-year-old Caliphate and, in Iberia, by a thin Visigothic elite in the middle of a civil war.

bridge: Chapter 1 laid out the board around the year 700: a shattered Mediterranean, a Byzantine Empire reeling from the loss of Syria and Egypt, and a Caliphate that in eighty years had conquered an arc from India's borders to Morocco. Its westernmost troops were not Arabs but recently Islamized Berbers, chafing under Arab commanders. Across the strait sat Visigothic Iberia — a thin Germanic warrior aristocracy ruling a Hispano-Roman Christian majority and a persecuted Jewish minority, with a law code, bishops' councils at Toledo, and a chronic habit of settling the succession by coup. In 711 it was doing exactly that.
setup: This is the conquest — and the puzzle is its speed. In spring 711 a Berber freedman named Tariq ibn Ziyad crosses with maybe 7,000 men, lands at the rock that takes his name (Jabal Tariq, mangled into Gibraltar), and within weeks the Visigothic king Roderic and his whole army vanish at a battle near the Guadalete. Within five years Tariq and his Arab superior Musa ibn Nusayr hold most of the peninsula. The interesting question is not how Tariq won one battle but why one lost battle ended a kingdom — and the answer is the mechanism behind everything that follows: a warrior elite nobody had reason to defend, replaced by conquerors offering a contract. That contract, the dhimma — keep your faith, pay a tax, accept a lower status — is the most important and most misrepresented thing in the early story, and most arguments about al-Andalus are really arguments about how to feel about it. The army doesn't stop at the Pyrenees, and a skirmish in the northern mountains plants an acorn nobody notices.

bridge: Chapter 2 ended with the peninsula in its permanent shape: a Muslim south and center, a thin Christian fringe in the wet northern mountains, and a frontier between them. But for its first forty years al-Andalus was only a far-western province of a world empire run from Damascus — chronically unstable, its governors changing every year or two, riven by the feud that runs under everything early: Arab against Berber, with the Berbers who did most of the conquering shoved onto the worst land. In 740 that exploded into a great Berber revolt. The province was a powder keg with no king. Then, two thousand miles away, an event in 750 changed everything.
setup: In 750 the Umayyad dynasty that ruled the whole Islamic world from Damascus was overthrown and massacred by the rival Abbasids — the event that splits the histories of the Islamic east and west. One Umayyad grandson got out. Abd al-Rahman, about twenty, fled the entire width of the Islamic world, hunted the whole way, reached his Berber mother's kin in Morocco, crossed into Spain in 755, and within a year made himself ruler of al-Andalus. He did not claim to be caliph — that meant total war he couldn't win — so he ruled as amir, founding the independent Emirate of Córdoba in 756 while still naming the distant Abbasid caliph in Friday prayers, a thin fiction of unity. This is the hinge: the Islamic far west becomes a state, not a province, ruled by a refugee dynasty with a grievance. His most consequential act wasn't a battle but a building — the Great Mosque of Córdoba, modeled on the lost mosque of Damascus. He was building Syria in Spain.

bridge: Chapter 3 turned al-Andalus from a province into an independent state — the Emirate of Córdoba, founded by the runaway Umayyad Abd al-Rahman I in 756 and announced to the world by the Great Mosque he began building. By 800 the board was set: a Umayyad state in the south ruling a population that was still mostly not Muslim, a clutch of small Christian kingdoms along the northern rim, and a frontier everyone assumed was permanent. But a state and a society are not the same thing, and the ninth century is where the conquest has to become a country.
setup: This is the chapter where al-Andalus stops being a conquest and starts being a society — painfully, violently, and so slowly that nobody living through it could see the shape. Two stories carry it. First, the Córdoba martyrs: between 850 and 859 around four dozen Christians sought out execution by publicly insulting the Prophet, a protest not against persecution but against assimilation, against a generation of Christian young men so Arabized they could write polished Arabic verse but not a decent Latin letter. Second, Umar ibn Hafsun, a convert-descended rebel who held the mountain fortress of Bobastro against the Emirate for forty years and nearly brought the state down. Underneath both runs the largest, slowest process in the whole narrative: how a country becomes Muslim — not by the sword, which the pact forbade, but by incentive, prestige, intermarriage, and time. The historian Richard Bulliet's S-curve suggests Muslims became a majority only around the year 1000 — three centuries after the conquest.

bridge: The ninth century (Chapter 4) left the Emirate at its weakest: the long Ibn Hafsun revolt and a scatter of others had shrunk Córdoba's real control to little more than Córdoba itself, the country was still mostly non-Muslim, and the old conqueror-versus-convert wound was wide open. The state the Falcon built looked like it might simply dissolve into warlord territory. Then in 912 a twenty-one-year-old inherited the wreck.
setup: Abd al-Rahman III — the Falcon's great-great-great-great-grandson, and by the chronicles' description red-haired and blue-eyed after generations of northern concubine mothers — ruled for forty-nine years, the longest reign in the story, and is the closest thing al-Andalus has to a colossus. His first two decades were the methodical reconquest of his own kingdom. Then, around 929, he did the single most important symbolic act in the political narrative: he proclaimed himself Caliph, a claim of universal Muslim leadership the Córdoban Umayyads had pointedly avoided for two centuries. The trigger was a third caliphate — the Shia Fatimids, expanding across the strait in North Africa toward Córdoba's own Berber recruiting grounds. Now the Mediterranean had three rival caliphs at once. He backed the title with Madinat al-Zahra, a purpose-built palace-city designed to make caliphal power legible, and a gold dinar trusted across the western Mediterranean. Byzantine and German emperors sent embassies. The only question was whether the machine could outlive the man.

bridge: Abd al-Rahman III (Chapter 5) spent two decades reconquering his own kingdom, then in 929 proclaimed himself Caliph and built Madinat al-Zahra to prove it, turning a state that barely ran Córdoba into the most advanced city in western Europe — embassies, a trusted gold coin, a salaried army. When he died in 961 the machine was at its zenith. His successor had spent that entire forty-nine-year reign waiting in middle age, and what he wanted when his turn finally came was not conquest.
setup: Al-Hakam II ruled only fifteen short, peaceful years, but they tell you more about what this civilization valued than almost anything else. He wanted books. The number usually given for his caliphal library is four hundred thousand volumes — treat it the way you treat all medieval book-counts, but the comparison is the point: the best monastic libraries of Latin Europe counted their books in the hundreds. He ran agents in the markets of Baghdad, Cairo, and Damascus to buy or copy new works, sometimes acquiring a book before its author's own city had it. He funded twenty-seven free schools where Córdoba's poor children learned to read at state expense, with essentially no parallel in Latin Europe. He also completed the most beautiful phase of the Great Mosque, its new mihrab sheathed in gold mosaic by Greek Christian craftsmen sent from Constantinople — a Christian gift to a Muslim rival's mosque. But the library is the real point: it is the infrastructure of the intellectual transmission al-Andalus is most genuinely important for. When al-Hakam died in 976, the heir was eleven years old, and the army now followed whoever paid it.

bridge: Chapter 6 ended the Caliphate at its zenith and showed the crack in it: al-Hakam II, the book-collecting caliph, died in 976 leaving an eleven-year-old heir, Hisham II, in a state whose army — Berber regiments and imported European slave-soldiers — now followed whoever paid and commanded it rather than any sacred bloodline. Abd al-Rahman III had built that professional army to free the dynasty from the old Arab clans. Into the gap a child-caliph opened, a man walked who would take al-Andalus to the peak of its military terror and guarantee its destruction.
setup: His name was Muhammad ibn Abi Amir; history knows him by his self-awarded title al-Mansur, 'the Victorious,' which Christian Spain turned into Almanzor. He was not royal — an ambitious official who climbed through the palace, attached himself to the boy-caliph's mother, and by about 981 ruled al-Andalus absolutely, while carefully keeping Hisham II as a sacred figurehead he never deposed. His instrument was the razzia, the fast destructive raid: some fifty near-annual campaigns, almost none lost, sacking Barcelona in 985 and the great pilgrimage shrine of Santiago de Compostela in 997, whose bells he had carried to Córdoba on Christian captives' shoulders. To campaign every year he leaned on Berber regiments and slave-soldiers loyal only to the paymaster — a short-term solution that was a long-term poison. He died in 1002, and within seven years the structure detonated into the Fitna, a twenty-two-year civil war that burned Madinat al-Zahra and, in 1031, abolished the Caliphate outright. The most powerful state in the western Mediterranean killed itself.

bridge: Chapter 7 ended with the most powerful state in the western Mediterranean committing suicide: Almanzor's brilliant, paymaster-loyal army outlived his control, detonated into the twenty-two-year Fitna, burned Madinat al-Zahra, and in 1031 the leading citizens of Córdoba — with no credible caliph left to fight over — simply abolished the Caliphate. The unified power was gone. What replaced it is one of the strangest political-cultural configurations in medieval history.
setup: Al-Andalus did not fall to a conqueror in 1031; it dissolved, the way a corporation does, into the men already running its pieces. Governors, city families, regiment commanders each kept his chunk and declared himself its ruler — the taifa period, roughly two to three dozen rival Muslim city-states at each other's throats. Here is the paradox that makes it instructive: politically a catastrophe, culturally perhaps the most brilliant period al-Andalus ever had. With one central court gone there were now thirty courts, every petty king wanting to be Córdoba, competing through poets and palaces (the same machine Renaissance Italy would run four centuries later). But the machine had a fatal flaw: the parias, protection payments in gold that terrified taifa kings paid the rough Christian kingdoms of the north — the precise mechanism by which the south financed the north to grow strong enough to conquer it. In 1085 Alfonso VI of Castile took Toledo, the old Visigothic capital, permanently. Facing a choice between Christian vassalage and calling in the desert puritans of Morocco, Seville's poet-king al-Mu'tamid chose the desert.

bridge: The taifa century (Chapter 8) was a cultural golden age built on a fatal weakness: thirty disunited little kingdoms so terrified of each other that they paid protection gold — the parias — to the Christian north, financing the very powers that were eating them. When Alfonso VI took Toledo permanently in 1085, the racket reached its terminus. Seville's poet-king al-Mu'tamid, forced to choose between Christian vassalage and calling in the fearsome Muslim fundamentalists who had risen across the strait in Morocco, said he would rather drive camels in Africa than herd swine in Castile — and sent for the Almoravids.
setup: The power al-Mu'tamid summoned was the strangest army that ever fought in Spain, and it came out of the deep Sahara. The Almoravids were veiled Sanhaja Berber camel nomads — desert puritans welded into a conquest state by a stern preacher, ruling Morocco from their new capital Marrakesh, as far from the silk-and-poetry world of Seville as you can get while sharing a religion. Their commander Yusuf ibn Tashfin crossed in 1086 and crushed Alfonso VI at Sagrajas (Zallaqa), checking the Christian advance hard. Then he looked at the taifa kings, judged them no true Muslims — wine-drinkers, love-poets, tribute-payers to infidels — and between 1090 and 1094 conquered the taifas themselves, deposing the very kings who had invited him. Al-Mu'tamid died a prisoner in a Moroccan oasis, writing exile poetry about his daughters in rags. Al-Andalus was a province again, ruled from Marrakesh. And the pattern that will repeat: the desert puritans grew comfortable within two generations, and the next desert movement would say of them exactly what they had said of the taifa kings.

bridge: Chapter 9 brought the Almoravids — veiled Saharan puritans — across the strait to check the Christian advance at Sagrajas in 1086, then to swallow the very taifa kingdoms that had summoned them, deposing the poet-king al-Mu'tamid and ruling al-Andalus as a province of Morocco. But the chapter ended with a pattern stated as a warning: the desert puritans grew comfortable within two generations, leaned on a rigid faction of jurists, even burned the books of the great theologian al-Ghazali — and in the Atlas Mountains a new preacher was denouncing them as corrupt and barely Muslim. The wheel was turning again.
setup: The movement that destroyed the Almoravids began with one man's theology. Ibn Tumart, an Atlas Berber, absorbed al-Ghazali's rigorous theology, came home radicalized, preached the absolute oneness of God (tawhid), and had himself proclaimed the Mahdi — the awaited divine redeemer, a claim that turns a reform movement into a militant church it is unbelief to oppose. His followers were the al-Muwahhidun, 'those who affirm the oneness,' which Europe turned into Almohads. His ablest successor, the genius commander Abd al-Mu'min, destroyed the Almoravids, took Marrakesh in 1147, and built the largest single empire the Islamic west ever produced. The Almohads present the narrative's central paradox at its sharpest: they largely abolished the protected-minority dhimma — convert, exile, or death — and it was fleeing them that Maimonides left Córdoba. Yet the same fundamentalist century is the century of Averroes flourishing under the same caliphs' patronage. Tolerant golden age and persecuting empire describe the same regime. They built the Giralda and won big at Alarcos in 1195 — their brief high-water mark, just before the Christian kingdoms finally united.

bridge: The Almohads (Chapter 10) were the largest empire the Islamic west ever produced and the most ideologically rigid regime in the whole story — abolishing the protected-minority pact, patronizing Averroes while crushing the Jews, building the Giralda, winning big at Alarcos in 1195. That victory was the high-water mark, and it was brief. The Christian kingdoms of the north — Castile, Aragon, Navarre, Portugal — were normally too busy fighting each other to combine. In 1212, with the Pope declaring the war a crusade, they finally did the one thing the south could not survive: they united.
setup: On July 16, 1212, on a high plain called Las Navas de Tolosa, the combined armies of Castile, Aragon, and Navarre destroyed the Almohad field army — the single most decisive battle in the entire eight-century story, after which everything happens in its shadow. The timing carries a brutal irony: only eight years earlier, in 1204, a Catholic crusader army had sacked Christian Constantinople, so the cross triumphed in the west exactly as it wounded itself in the east. What followed was so fast contemporaries felt it as an unmaking: with no Almohad army left, the great cities fell in a single generation — Córdoba in 1236, Valencia in 1238, Seville in 1248. In about twenty-five years al-Andalus shrank to a single mountain kingdom around Granada. Two things outlast the conquest. The conquered Muslims became Mudéjars, given a deal structurally identical to the old dhimma — coexistence running both directions under both faiths. And the conquerors inherited cities full of Arabic books, which in Toledo became medieval Europe's greatest translation enterprise. The political conquest of al-Andalus is also the moment Europe absorbed its mind.

bridge: The narrative has now run the political story all the way from Tariq's crossing in 711 to the Great Reconquista of the 1240s (Chapter 11), which broke al-Andalus down to a single surviving kingdom and, in the process, created Muslims-under-Christian-rule (Mudéjars) living the mirror image of the Christians-under-Muslim-rule (Mozarabs) of the early centuries. Coexistence, it turns out, ran both directions under both faiths. The book has been deferring the question underneath all of it — the convivencia argument flagged in Chapter 1 — and steps out of the war to take it head-on.
setup: This is the chapter everyone fights about, and the honest way to write it is not to deliver a verdict but to lay out the machinery and show why intelligent people reach opposite conclusions from the same evidence. The legal foundation was the dhimma: Christians and Jews as protected but subordinate — keep your faith, pay the jizya, accept an inferior status that could mean distinctive dress, no weapons, no authority over Muslims. It was tolerated inequality in the original sense: permitted to exist, not regarded as equal. The Jewish 'Golden Age' is where the utopia claim is strongest — Hasdai ibn Shaprut a caliph's diplomat, Samuel ibn Naghrillah a practicing Jew running a Muslim kingdom's government and army — and also where its limits are sharpest: in 1066 the Muslims of Granada massacred the Jewish community, and the Almohads later shattered Jewish and Christian life entirely. The defensible synthesis, which this chapter commits to: a working multi-religious civilization built on inequality, safer than Christian Europe at the same time and never equal — harder to merchandise, and more interesting, than either cartoon.

bridge: Chapter 12 took the convivencia debate head-on and landed on a synthesis: al-Andalus as a working multi-religious civilization built on inequality. But the chapter also pointed past itself — what that society actually produced with its three faiths and shared language is a separate question, and one where the evidence is far less ambiguous. Chapter 6 already planted the seed: al-Hakam II's enormous Córdoba library, the single richest concentration of books in western Eurasia, the infrastructure this chapter finally pays off.
setup: Strip away the argument and one fact stands alone: for roughly three centuries al-Andalus was one of the few places on Earth where the ancient world's scientific knowledge was not just preserved but advanced — and the only such place in physical contact with Latin Europe. The substrate was the eastern Islamic tradition flowing west: the Greek corpus (Aristotle, Euclid, Ptolemy, Galen) and Indian mathematics, all rendered into Arabic in Baghdad, then imported wholesale by Córdoba's library. On top of it, Andalusi scholars did original work. The Toledo astronomer al-Zarqali compiled the most accurate astronomical tables in the West for two centuries, cited into Copernicus's time. Al-Zahrawi's illustrated surgery stayed the standard European textbook for six hundred years. New crops — rice, citrus, sugar, cotton, eggplant — and the irrigation to grow them entered Europe through Spain, leaving roughly eight percent of Spanish vocabulary Arabic. And the payoff is concrete: when Christians took the Andalusi cities, especially Toledo, named translators like Gerard of Cremona rendered the Arabic books into Latin. Al-Andalus matters to science not because it had clever men but because it was the loading dock through which the ancient world re-entered the West.

bridge: Chapter 13 established al-Andalus as the loading dock: the place where the ancient world's science was preserved, advanced, and — through the Toledo translators working on captured Arabic books — physically re-entered Latin Europe. That pipeline carried more than astronomical tables and surgical manuals. It carried philosophy, and one philosopher above all. The same Córdoba library and the same Toledo translation enterprise that moved the sciences moved the minds, and the minds are the strongest single case for the civilization's world-historical importance.
setup: One man from al-Andalus taught Latin Europe how to read Aristotle, and that alone would earn it a permanent place in Western thought — but it produced a whole constellation, Muslim and Jewish. The range is real: Ibn Hazm the literalist jurist who also wrote the tenderest book on love; Ibn Tufayl, whose desert-island novel about whether unaided reason can reach truth predates Robinson Crusoe by five and a half centuries. The summit is Averroes (Ibn Rushd), born in Córdoba in 1126, a judge under the same Almohad caliphs whose regime was crushing the Jews. His close commentaries recovered what Aristotle actually argued; to the Latin schoolmen he was simply 'the Commentator,' capital C, no name needed. A dead end in the later Islamic world, his work detonated in the Christian universities — Aquinas's whole synthesis is unimaginable without him. The Jewish parallel is Maimonides, born in the same city twelve years later, driven out by Almohad persecution, thriving under Saladin in Cairo, attempting the same Aristotelian synthesis for Judaism. Two philosophers, three religions, one Spanish city — and the mind ran east too, into Sufism, through Ibn Arabi.

bridge: The last two chapters made the case for al-Andalus as a transmitter — the loading dock for ancient science (Chapter 13) and the home of Averroes and Maimonides, the minds that reshaped Europe's thought (Chapter 14). But a civilization is not only its battles and philosophers. It is what it built, sang, and ate — and on this al-Andalus left more surviving physical evidence than on almost anything else, which makes this the chapter where the romantic and documented versions come closest to agreeing, because the buildings are still standing.
setup: Begin with the Great Mosque of Córdoba, the deepest single text the civilization left and the building Chapter 3 promised to return to. Walk in and you are in a forest of columns — many Roman and Visigothic spoils reused to say the new order inherits Rome — carrying double-tiered horseshoe arches in red-and-white stripes, repeating until the room seems edgeless, a built argument about the infinity of God. The horseshoe arch itself was a Visigothic form the conquerors adopted, evidence in stone that al-Andalus synthesized on the spot rather than importing wholesale from Damascus. The same grammar runs through Madinat al-Zahra, the Giralda, and the Alhambra: geometry, water as architecture, the courtyard garden built as an image of the Quranic paradise — the direct ancestor of the Spanish patio, word included. The sound left two genuine inventions: the muwashshah song-poem, whose closing kharja, often a woman's voice in early Romance, is among the oldest surviving lyric in any Romance language. Whether it influenced the troubadours is a genuinely contested argument, suggestive but thin. And Ziryab, the musician of legend, is the kind of too-perfect 'one man civilized them' story to hold very loosely.

bridge: Chapter 11 broke al-Andalus down to a single surviving piece after Las Navas de Tolosa and the avalanche of conquests — Córdoba, Valencia, and Seville all gone within a generation. The three thematic chapters since then stepped out of the chronology to weigh the three faiths, the sciences, and the philosophers. Now the narrative returns to the war it left, and to the one fragment that did not fall: a mountain kingdom in the southeast that survived not by being strong but by being clever, useful, and lucky.
setup: The survivor was the Emirate of Granada, ruled by the Nasrid dynasty from 1238 to 1492 — surviving 254 years, longer than the Caliphate and the Almoravid and Almohad periods combined. It existed because of a bargain at its birth: in 1246 its founder Muhammad I became the vassal of Ferdinand III of Castile, paying enormous tribute and even helping a Christian army take Muslim Seville in 1248. That is the unsentimental foundation of the 'last paradise.' What followed was a masterpiece of weak-state diplomacy: pay tribute when forced, withhold it when Castile was distracted, play the Moroccan Marinids against Castile, exploit every Christian succession crisis, switch sides, endure. It worked because no Christian power had both the unity and the will to finish the job. The kingdom was also densely cultured and rich on silk and Saharan gold, and its monument is the Alhambra — overwhelming through cheap materials and surface alone, its walls covered in Quranic verse and original poetry that describes the very rooms it is carved in. Ibn al-Khatib argued from observation that the Black Death spread by contagion. Ibn Battuta passed through and found a kingdom still confident, with a century and a half to run.

bridge: Chapter 16 left Nasrid Granada as the last kingdom — a small, clever, tribute-paying client that survived 254 years by exploiting Christian disunity, playing Castile against Morocco, and switching sides at every crisis. Its scholars still argued out the science of plague, its Alhambra still narrated itself in carved poetry, and Ibn Battuta found it confident with a century and a half left to run. The chapter ended on the one thing that could undo all of it: the two great Christian crowns of the peninsula finally combining.
setup: The end came in a single decade, and it came because of a marriage. In 1469 Isabella, heir to Castile, married Ferdinand, heir to Aragon — the Catholic Monarchs, the first time the two largest Christian kingdoms were ruled as one coordinated power. For 254 years Granada had survived on Christian disunity; in 1469 the disunity ended. The Granada War ran 1482 to 1492, a methodical town-by-town reduction with siege artillery the Nasrids could not match, helped fatally by a three-way Nasrid civil war among the emir, his brother, and his son Boabdil — whom the Monarchs played against his own family. When Málaga resisted, its surviving population was killed or enslaved almost entirely, a demonstration of the cost of resistance. On January 2, 1492, Boabdil handed over the keys of the Alhambra: 801 years after Tariq landed, no Muslim state remained in western Europe. But the year is loaded for what else this same triumphant state did from the same camp — in March the Alhambra Decree expelled the Jews; that spring it funded Columbus. The end of the Iberian Middle Ages and the start of the European conquest of the world are, quite literally, the same season.

bridge: Chapter 17 ended on January 2, 1492, with Boabdil handing over the keys of the Alhambra and the last Muslim state in western Europe gone — and on the surrender treaty, the Capitulations of Granada, which promised the Muslims of Granada their religion, mosques, law, and language, the old dhimma logic now running in reverse. That same loaded year also expelled the Jews and funded Columbus. But a civilization does not end the day its last king hands over the keys. It ends over the following century, in what is done to the people who stayed — and this is where the romantic version goes quietest.
setup: The Capitulations lasted less than a decade. From 1499 Cardinal Cisneros pushed mass forced conversion, Quran burnings, and the systematic dismantling of the promises; a revolt gave the crown its pretext, and by 1502 the Muslims of Castile were ordered to convert or leave. The converted and their descendants — Christian by law, suspected of secret Islam in fact — became the Moriscos, Spain's internal scapegoat for a century: forbidden their language, dress, and names, periodically rebelling (the War of the Alpujarras, crushed in 1571), never trusted, never assimilated, never left alone. The end came in 1609–1614, when the crown expelled an estimated three hundred thousand Moriscos — most born in Spain, baptized Christians, rooted in Iberia for generations, some descended from converts of the ninth century — shipped to a North Africa they had never seen, often unable to speak Arabic. That, not 1492, is the literal end of al-Andalus. What survived was the physical heritage (Washington Irving's 1832 'Tales of the Alhambra' fixed its romantic image) and the argument — al-Andalus as the screen onto which the modern world still projects its hopes and fears.
